title: How Zendia Shops
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Shopping has changed more in the last twenty years than in the previous two hundred. In the imaginary country of Zendia, the national statistics office has measured the way in which people buy goods since 1995, and its figures show clear and very different trends in four kinds of shopping. This passage describes them and considers the reasons, for businesses and for customers. It also asks what the figures may suggest about the next twenty years. Its authors point out that the figures include only goods bought in Zendia, and that purchases made on foreign websites, which are growing quickly, are not yet counted in the same way.

Online clothes shopping is the clearest case of growth. In 1995, it was almost unknown, because few households owned a computer. The share of clothes bought on the internet has risen every year since, and it now accounts for more than a third of all clothing sales. Free delivery and easy returns have been important, since customers can try the goods at home and send back anything that does not fit, which has removed an important reason for caution.

High-street shops, which sell goods in towns, have followed the opposite path. Their share of all sales was above ninety per cent in 1995, and it has fallen without a pause ever since. Many well-known stores have closed, and rows of empty premises are now a common sight in the centres of smaller towns. Local councils have tried to help by lowering parking charges and by arranging markets and events, but with little effect so far.

Paper catalogues, which once arrived in every home and offered goods by post, show a pattern with a peak. Orders grew until about 2002, helped by the arrival of telephone ordering and credit cards. After that, they began to fall, as customers moved to websites, which offer a wider choice and more up-to-date prices. The largest catalogue company stopped printing its paper edition in 2016, and it now exists only online.

The last case is grocery delivery, which changed little for many years. Supermarkets began to offer it in the early 2000s, but few customers used it, and the share of orders remained close to zero for more than a decade. Then, in 2020, when many people were advised to stay at home, the share jumped abruptly. It has remained higher than before, though it has not yet fallen back, which suggests that many people have found a habit they wish to keep.

Why do these four cases differ so much? Dr Anna Ivanova, a retail economist, believes that the answer lies in how easily the experience of buying can be copied on a screen. Clothes can be returned and compared, and catalogues are already pictures, so both moved online easily. Fresh food is harder, because customers like to choose it themselves. Dr Ivanova adds that events such as the stay-at-home period can change habits permanently, and that firms should expect more surprises.

For town centres, the lesson is that they must offer something that a screen cannot, such as meeting friends, enjoying a meal or attending an event. A number of towns have already turned former shops into homes, libraries and small workshops. Retailers, too, are experimenting, combining a website with shops that let customers collect their orders on the same day. Estate agents report that former shops in good locations are now rented for cafes, gyms and health centres, which attract many more visitors than a clothes shop did. It is too early to say which model will succeed, but nobody expects a return to the situation of 1995.
